label: Gradient Flows in Wasserstein Space
notes: This chapter opens the gradient-flow story that occupies printed pages 629 through 692. We treat the space of probability measures as a curved metric space under the quadratic Wasserstein distance, and we read evolution equations as curves running downhill along an energy functional. The heat equation will become our first concrete example.

label: Steepest Descent Reconsidered
notes: Before lifting to measures, recall how steepest descent works on a manifold. The velocity points opposite to the Riemannian gradient, so the energy falls as fast as the metric allows. Wasserstein gradient flows copy this picture exactly, but the manifold is now an infinite-dimensional space of densities equipped with a transport metric.

label: The Energy Functional
notes: Gradient flows need an energy to descend. We focus on free-energy functionals built from an internal entropy term, a potential, and an interaction. The internal term uses a convex density function; choosing the Boltzmann entropy makes the resulting flow the linear heat equation. Different energies select different evolution equations from the same scheme.

label: Wasserstein as a Riemannian Metric
notes: Otto's calculus reads the Wasserstein space as formally Riemannian. Tangent vectors are infinitesimal mass displacements written as continuity-equation velocity fields, and the metric measures their kinetic energy. This viewpoint lets us define gradients of functionals and gives meaning to the phrase steepest descent in the space of probability measures.

label: The JKO Minimizing-Movement Scheme
notes: Jordan, Kinderlehrer, and Otto proposed building the flow one small step at a time. Each step minimizes the energy plus a quadratic penalty equal to the squared Wasserstein distance to the previous density, divided by twice the time step. This is the proximal point method, transplanted from Euclidean optimization into the transport metric.

label: The Proximal Step in W2
notes: Read the JKO update as a proximal operator. The penalty keeps the new measure close to the old one in transport distance, while the energy term pulls it downhill. As the step size shrinks the penalty dominates short moves, so the discrete trajectory hugs the true gradient-flow curve more and more tightly.

label: Descending the Energy Landscape
notes: Here is the geometric heart of the scheme. The minimizing-movement iterates form a staircase descending the energy surface, each tread a single Wasserstein proximal step. Refining the time step turns the staircase into a smooth curve of steepest descent, the continuous gradient flow we ultimately want to construct.

label: Heat Equation as Entropy Gradient Flow
notes: The headline identity: the heat equation is the gradient flow of the Boltzmann entropy in Wasserstein space. Adding a confining potential turns it into the Fokker-Planck equation, the gradient flow of the corresponding free energy. A single variational principle thus produces a whole family of diffusion equations.

label: Euler-Lagrange of One Step
notes: Differentiating a single JKO step gives its optimality condition. The first variation of the Wasserstein penalty produces a Kantorovich potential, whose gradient is the optimal transport velocity. Setting the total variation to zero recovers a discrete continuity equation that, in the limit, becomes the continuous diffusion equation we expect.

label: Energy Dissipation Estimate
notes: The scheme comes with a free a-priori bound. Summing the optimality of each step telescopes into an energy-dissipation inequality controlling the total squared distance travelled by the discrete curve. This uniform estimate is exactly the compactness we need to pass to the limit and extract a continuous trajectory.

label: Existence by Minimizing Movements
notes: Compactness plus lower semicontinuity finishes the construction. The piecewise-constant and interpolated JKO curves converge to an absolutely continuous curve in Wasserstein space that solves the gradient-flow equation. Minimizing movements thus prove existence for the heat and Fokker-Planck flows without ever differentiating the equation directly.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We assembled the gradient-flow toolkit: a free energy, the Wasserstein metric, and the JKO proximal scheme stepping downhill to build solutions. The heat and Fokker-Planck equations emerged as entropy gradient flows, with existence proved by minimizing movements. The sequel sharpens this into contraction and convexity estimates governed by Ricci curvature.
